newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Ireland election winner to press for IRA truce.
newsitem.headline: Ireland election winner to press for IRA truce.

text.p: The Northern Ireland peace process, mired for a year in the very conflicts it was supposed to end, will receive fresh attention this month following the narrow Irish election victory of Fianna Fail's Bertie Ahern.
"The possibilities of moving forward are tremendous," said Ahern, as he and his Progressive Democrat allies won 81 seats, two short of the majority needed to govern.

His narrow win, together with the election of Tony Blair with a huge majority as British Prime Minister last month, will bring new pressure to bear on Northern Ireland's pro-British Unionist and pro-Irish nationalists to reach a settlement.
Their Belfast talks have been bogged down for a year by procedural based on fundamental distrust between majority Protestants and minority Catholics.
Ahern said that former Prime Minister Albert Reynolds, who helped launch the peace process by securing an IRA cease-fire in 1994, would be a special Northern Ireland envoy.

Ahern said Northern Ireland was, with tax cuts and crime, one of his three top priorities and planned to meet the leader of the IRA's Sinn Fein political wing, Gerry Adams, over the next week, "if that is feasible".
He told reporters that he would be pressing Adams to secure a new cease-fire by his Irish Republican Army guerrilla allies in their war against British rule of Northern Ireland.

The Ahern-Adams meeting must take place before parliament reconvenes on June 26 to elect Ahern Prime Minister because the official position of Britain, Ireland and the United States is to ban top-level contact until the IRA restores its truce.
"I said I would not meet Mr Adams after becoming Taoiseach (Prime Minister)," Ahern said.
Sinn Fein believes Ahern, whose party casts itself as the genuine voice of Irish republicanism, will be easier to work with than his predecessor, party sources said.
But Sinn Fein has shown no sign of changing its demand for automatic inclusion in the Northern Ireland peace process without a new IRA truce by virtue of its success in British and Irish elections.
Ahern ruled out any electoral survival deal with the Sinn Fein candidate, Caoimhghin O Caolain, who won a seat in the border constituency of Cavan Monaghan .
Adams and his chief strategist, Martin McGuinness won British parliamentary seats last month which they refuse to occupy because it would entail an oath of allegiance to Britain.
But O Caolain will occupy his new seat in Dublin, where the party ended a policy of boycotting the house in 1986.
Ahern said ending IRA violence was the key to progress at Belfast peace talks from which Sinn Fein is barred because of continuing IRA violence.
"It is very hard to get anywhere as long as there is violence. I have said this to Gerry Adams, and I have said it to many other people," Ahern said.

Like his predecessor, John Bruton, U.S. President Bill Clinton and two British premiers, Ahern challenged Sinn Fein to prove the meaning of its "peace strategy" by securing a new truce to replace the one the IRA broke in February 1996.
"They have stated in the elections, here and in the north, that there is a peace strategy. I think they have to prove that now," Ahern told state broadcaster RTE.

As far as I am concerned, if they prove their part, I will do everything I humanly can to move the peace process forward. But I cannot do an awful lot of things I would like to do unless there is peace," he said."
